query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-based alloys, the mechanical property differences are governed by two related mechanisms: (1) increased local lattice distortion, quantified by MSAD, which raises the 0 K CRSS through enhanced solid-solution strengthening at low temperatures, and (2) an additional strengthening increment at high temperatures due to dynamic elastic solute pinning (predominantly by Mn and Fe) that produces serrated flow via a Cottrell-type mechanism.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized, water-quenched equiatomic FCC single crystals (quinary, quaternary, and ternary derivatives) of Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-based medium-entropy alloys, processed by Bridgman or optical floating-zone methods and annealed for 168 h at 1273 or 1473 K.
generation.intervention: Compression testing along the [1̄23] orientation to determine CRSS for (111)[1̄01] slip, including temperature-dependent measurements, strain-rate jump tests, TEM imaging of dislocations, and DFT calculations of MSAD.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted in compression from 9 to 1373 K at an engineering strain rate of 1 × 10^-4 s^-1, with strain-rate jumps below room temperature (down to 1 × 10^-2 s^-1) during Stage I deformation (≈10% plastic strain) and specific exclusion of data points below each alloy’s inertial-critical temperature and above 873 K where the PL effect begins.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions (measured by MSAD) which modify the dislocation glide-resistance landscape; in Cr-containing alloys these distortions are larger, and in high-temperature regimes, diffusible Mn- and Fe-rich solutes promote elastic dislocation pinning.
generation.mechanism: Below room temperature, plastic deformation is dominated by thermally activated dislocation glide that is hindered by solid-solution obstacles arising from lattice distortions, while at elevated temperatures (around 673 to 973 K) dynamic solute pinning results in a modest increase in CRSS and serrated flow due to a Cottrell-type elastic interaction between dislocations and solute atmospheres.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, alloys with higher MSAD (notably those containing Cr) will exhibit higher extrapolated 0 K CRSS values, and alloys richer in Mn and Fe will show a larger high-temperature CRSS increment and pronounced PL serrated flow. Furthermore, cooling below room temperature will result in a substantial CRSS increase (with a less steep rise below ~77 K due to the onset of inertial effects), while heating into the diffusion-active regime will lead to a modest additional strengthening compared to the room-temperature baseline.
generation.baseline: Room-temperature CRSS for the quinary equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and similar measurements from CrFeCoNi/CrCoNi single crystals serve as benchmarks for comparison.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to equiatomic FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-based single crystals processed under controlled thermomechanical and annealing conditions, evaluated in compression along the [1̄23] orientation. It is valid in the thermally activated regime below room temperature (excluding temperatures where dislocation inertia dominates) and in the intermediate regime up to about 873 K before large PL effects and dynamic solute pinning become dominant.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative scaling of MSAD with CRSS and the relative contribution of solute pinning versus lattice distortion in non-Cr-containing variants is uncertain, as is the precise temperature range over which inertial effects blunt the CRSS increase at cryogenic temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform temperature-dependent compression tests on equiatomic and derivative single crystals across the 9–1373 K range. Determine CRSS from 0.2% offset yield stress and verify slip systems via slip-trace identification. Use strain-rate jump tests below room temperature to detect inertial effects, and observe serrated flow and CRSS increments at high temperatures indicative of PL behavior. TEM should assess dislocation structures and partial separation (for evidence against Suzuki segregation). Finally, correlate extrapolated 0 K CRSS (τ₀/μ) with sqrt(MSAD)/b across different compositions.
measurements: Temperature-dependent CRSS from 0.2% offset yield stress
Strain-rate sensitivity and apparent activation volumes from strain-rate jump tests
Observation of stress–strain serrations during high-temperature tests
TEM measurements of dislocation core structures and partial-dislocation dissociation widths
Correlation analysis between MSAD values (from DFT) and extrapolated τ₀/μ
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with higher calculated MSAD do not exhibit consistently higher extrapolated 0 K CRSS and/or if increased Mn and Fe content does not correlate with a measurable increase in the high-temperature CRSS increment and pronounced serrated flow (PL effect), the hypothesis would be rejected.
